justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a relatively stable near-term outlook with modest upward drift over longer horizons. For the one-day estimate of around 260.5, I was anchoring heavily on the most recent price or index level, assuming mean-reversion tendencies and low intraday volatility would keep movement contained. The one-week estimate of 261 is nearly flat versus the daily, reflecting the idea that short-term momentum is roughly neutral and that no major catalysts were obviously pending. The one-month estimate nudges slightly higher to 263, incorporating a mild upward bias that often characterizes equity or risk-asset benchmarks over multi-week periods when no recession or crisis signal is present — essentially a small risk premium drift embedded into the forecast.

The confidence interval widths expand significantly as the horizon lengthens, which is the standard result of uncertainty compounding over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans only 15 points, reflecting that daily realized volatility is relatively constrained and most sessions close within a narrow band of the open. By one week, the interval widens to 28 points, capturing the possibility of a meaningful macro data release, a central bank communication shift, or a geopolitical development that could shift sentiment. The one-month interval stretches to 57 points, acknowledging that over four or so weeks, a full repricing of rate expectations, an earnings season surprise, or a change in global risk appetite could materially alter the level.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes outside even these wider intervals. On the downside, an unexpected credit event, a sharper-than-anticipated inflation print prompting aggressive central bank action, or an escalation in geopolitical conflict could produce a rapid drawdown well below 235. On the upside, a dovish policy pivot, a strong batch of economic data signaling a soft landing, or a short-squeeze dynamic in heavily shorted assets could push above 292. Liquidity conditions also matter — thin markets around holidays or quarter-end rebalancing can amplify moves in either direction, making tail outcomes more probable than standard volatility models would suggest. These fat-tail risks are the primary reason I kept the intervals relatively generous even at the one-day horizon.
